name: Follistatin-344

lead: Follistatin-344 refers to a form of the protein follistatin (the 344 label is used by peptide vendors) sold as an experimental myostatin blocker. Follistatin is a natural protein that binds and neutralizes myostatin and activins.
Gene therapy work in animals and early clinical trials shows muscle effects, but no credible human evidence exists for injected peptide products.

paras: Follistatin binds myostatin and activin, preventing them from signalling through their receptors, which relieves the brake on muscle growth in animal models.

Not approved; banned in sport. Because follistatin affects reproductive hormones and other tissues, blocking these pathways raises theoretical concerns. Marketed peptides are unregulated and may not contain what is claimed.

lead: Follistatin-344 (often written FS-344) is the label under which unapproved, injectable preparations of the protein follistatin are sold by peptide vendors, mainly to people interested in building muscle. Follistatin itself is a secreted glycoprotein encoded by the FST gene in humans; it binds and neutralizes members of the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) superfamily, notably activin and myostatin (also called GDF-8), a protein that limits muscle growth.[1][2]

The appeal of the product in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles rests on animal research in which blocking myostatin, either by gene knockout or by raising follistatin levels, produced larger muscles.[1][3] Human work with follistatin has so far consisted of gene-therapy studies, in which a viral vector or plasmid delivers the follistatin gene, rather than injections of a purified peptide.[1][4] A 2026 narrative review of peptides marketed directly to patients for musculoskeletal injury and athletic performance included FS-344 among unapproved compounds and concluded that for many such peptides, favourable results come from animal models while rigorous human safety data are scarce.[5]
FS-344 is not approved as a medicine in any major jurisdiction, and community discussion of it on forums such as T Nation is mostly speculative about its effects and side effects.[6][7]

paras: Follistatin was originally identified in ovarian follicular fluid as a factor that suppressed secretion of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) from the pituitary, which is the origin of its name and its earlier label FSH-suppressing protein.[1][2] Later work showed it to be an activin-binding protein: a 1990 study purified an activin-binding protein from rat ovary and found it to be follistatin.[8] By the mid-1990s it was understood as a broader antagonist of TGF-beta family members, including bone morphogenetic proteins, and as a protein expressed in nearly all tissues, with highest concentrations in the ovary followed by skin.[1][2][9]

Several isoforms have been described. Wikipedia lists FS-288, FS-300 and FS-315, the first and third arising from alternative splicing and FS-300 (found in pigs) thought to arise from post-translational truncation.[1] One account of the gene's early cloning describes a precursor of 344 amino acids, which is the likely origin of the number in the vendor label, although the commercial naming is not defined in the primary literature cited here.[2] The circulating form is generally described as FS-315, and the cell-surface-associated form as FS-288.[2]

Follistatin is also involved in normal physiology beyond muscle: ovarian follicle development, embryonic patterning through inhibition of bone morphogenetic proteins, and inflammatory and tissue-repair responses.[1] Mice lacking the follistatin gene die soon after birth with defects that include insufficient muscle development and skeletal abnormalities.[9]

Myostatin is a TGF-beta family member that acts as a negative regulator of skeletal muscle mass.[10] Follistatin binds myostatin and activins and prevents them from engaging their cell-surface receptors, and structural studies describe an unusual induced-fit mechanism in which the ligand is held in a conformation that cannot signal.[2] A 2009 mouse study reported that follistatin-driven muscle hypertrophy involved satellite cell proliferation as well as inhibition of both myostatin and activin.[11]

Because follistatin binds activin as well as myostatin, researchers describe its effects as broader than selective myostatin blockade. Activin is involved in reproductive hormone signalling, and follistatin has roles in the ovary, skin and elsewhere, which is the basis for the concern, stated in reviews and forum discussion alike, that systemic follistatin exposure could affect tissues other than muscle.[1][4][5]

No published pharmacokinetic data on vendor-supplied FS-344 preparations in humans were found. Reviews of unapproved peptides note that composition, purity and dosing of gray-market products are not verified by regulators.[5]

No published clinical trials of injected, purified FS-344 peptide as sold by vendors were found. The human research that exists concerns follistatin gene therapy, in which the gene is delivered by a viral vector and the body produces the protein itself.

Wikipedia reports a clinical trial in sporadic inclusion body myositis in which an adeno-associated virus vector carrying the follistatin 344 gene (rAAV1.CMV.huFS344) was injected, and treated participants improved on a walking test compared with untreated controls, with reduced fibrosis and improved regeneration on biopsy.[1] Wikipedia also describes animal work: a 2009 study in macaque monkeys found that follistatin gene therapy increased muscle size and strength.[1]

Registered trials listed on ClinicalTrials.gov include a completed phase 1 study of an injectable follistatin plasmid gene therapy in 43 participants with frailty or ageing (NCT06411366), an early phase 1 study of combined klotho and follistatin gene therapy in 14 healthy adults (NCT07285629), and a phase 1/2 study of AAV-follistatin combined with a VEGF plasmid for age-related muscle decline (NCT07443826), which was listed as recruiting.[12][13][14] Published results of these registrations were not located.

ACE-083, a follistatin-based fusion protein, was investigated for focal muscle disorders; Wikipedia notes that in mice it increased growth and force in the injected muscle without systemic or endocrine effects.[1]

Many other human studies measure follistatin or follistatin-like proteins as biomarkers, for instance in obesity, cancer cachexia, or after exercise, rather than administering it.[15][16] Observational data summarized by Wikipedia associate higher circulating follistatin with increased risk of type 2 diabetes, heart failure, stroke, chronic kidney disease and earlier death, and describe a role for follistatin in insulin resistance and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; these are associations and do not indicate the effect of injecting the peptide.[1]

FS-344 is not an approved drug. The 2026 Sports Medicine review lists it among gray-market peptides that operate largely outside regulatory oversight and states that for many unapproved peptides, rigorous human safety data are scarce and serious harm is possible.[5]

Reviewers and forum participants raise theoretical concerns tied to follistatin biology: its effects on activin and reproductive hormones, its presence in many tissues, the observational links to metabolic and cardiovascular disease noted above, and its role in tumor microenvironments, where it is secreted and neutralizes TGF-beta ligands.[1] Forum users have also speculated about satellite cell depletion with long-term myostatin suppression.[17]
Product identity is a separate issue: vendor products are unregulated, and the review notes that unapproved peptides sold this way are not verified by regulators for content or purity.[5]

Pharmaceutical interest in the myostatin-activin-follistatin axis focuses on antibodies and receptor blockers. A 2024 review of weight-loss pharmacotherapy notes that bimagrumab, trevogrumab and garetosmab, which inhibit activin and myostatin signalling, have shown promise in reducing muscle loss while promoting fat loss, alone or with incretin drugs, and describes follistatin as a protein that opposes activin and myostatin to preserve lean mass during energy deficit.[18]
Follistatin gene therapy continues to be studied in muscle disease and ageing in early-phase trials, as listed above.[12][14]

On T Nation, follistatin appears from about 2007 as a speculative option: one 2007 reply to a question about a legitimate myostatin inhibitor said injected FS-344 "seems to have some promise" but was very new and its effects and side effects were unknown.[7] Later threads describe athletes getting injections, mention peptide clinics supplying it, or raise the idea of stacking it with growth hormone secretagogues or IGF-1 analogues.[6][17][19]

Forum users have also discussed non-injectable ways of raising follistatin, such as heavy training and certain foods or supplements, including a 2011 post attributing results to cocoa and a humorous 2010 post about eating pork skin.[20][21] No controlled evidence in the sources shows these approaches raising follistatin to a physiologically meaningful degree in muscle.

lore.intro: Follistatin appears in bodybuilding and peptide forums as a hoped-for route to myostatin blockade, usually discussed alongside other unapproved peptides.[6][7]

claims.claim: Injected FS-344 works as a myostatin inhibitor that adds muscle beyond natural limits

An activin-binding protein purified from rat ovary is identified as follistatin.[8]
